proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\), \(n>4r\), \(i\in I_n\), and \(w\in\{1,2\}\).  Couple the finite-volume wave to the restriction \(D^{(w)}|_{\Lambda_n}\) of the infinite assignment field, as prescribed by the buffered-restriction definition.  Since \(i\in I_n\),
\[
 \{i-r,\ldots,i+r\}\subseteq\Lambda_n. \tag{1}
\]
By the score-locality condition in the definition of \(\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\), the exposure and realized potential outcome entering \(Z_i^{(w)}\) are measurable functions only of \((U_j,D_j^{(w)})\) for the indices in (1).  The graph edge-range condition also ensures that restriction to \(\Lambda_n\) removes no neighbor of \(i\).  Hence the finite and infinite constructions use identical local innovations, assignment coordinates, graph neighborhood, exposure, and realized outcome.  Conditional on \(\mathcal F_U\), both constructions use the same product \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) law on the local assignment coordinates, so their conditional exposure probabilities coincide.  Exposure positivity makes both propensity denominators at least \(\varepsilon>0\).  Every factor in the two IPW formulas therefore agrees, and
\[
 Z_{n,i}^{(w)}=Z_i^{(w)}\qquad P\text{-almost surely}. \tag{2}
\]
Finally, \(\Lambda_n\setminus I_n\) consists of exactly the \(r\) left-end sites and the \(r\) right-end sites.  Since \(|\Lambda_n|=n\) and the locality radius \(r\) is fixed,
\[
 \frac{|\Lambda_n\setminus I_n|}{|\Lambda_n|}
 =\frac{2r}{n}\longrightarrow0.
\]
This proves both assertions.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  For either \(w\in\{1,2\}\), the score-decomposition definitions give
\[
 \xi_i^{(w)}+h_i
 =(Z_i^{(w)}-m_i)+(m_i-\tau_{\mathrm P})
 =Z_i^{(w)}-\tau_{\mathrm P}. \tag{1}
\]
Moreover, the definition \(m_i=\mathbb E_P[Z_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U]\) implies
\[
 \mathbb E_P[\xi_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U]=0. \tag{2}
\]
Because \(h_j=m_j-\tau_{\mathrm P}\) is \(\mathcal F_U\)-measurable, the tower and pull-out properties of conditional expectation yield
\[
 \mathbb E_P[\xi_i^{(w)}h_j]
 =\mathbb E_P\!\left[h_j\mathbb E_P(\xi_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U)\right]
 =0. \tag{3}
\]
The required integrability follows from the envelope proved next.  If \(e_1\ne e_0\), at most one of the two exposure indicators in the score is one.  The outcome envelope and exposure positivity therefore imply
\[
 |Z_i^{(w)}|
 \le \frac{|Y_i(D^{(w)};U,G)|}
 {\min\{\pi_i(e_1),\pi_i(e_0)\}}
 \le \frac B\varepsilon=K
 \qquad P\text{-almost surely}. \tag{4}
\]
If \(e_1=e_0\), the two terms in the score bracket cancel identically, so (4) again holds.  In particular, \(Z_i^{(w)}\), its conditional expectation \(m_i\), and all products in (3) are integrable; indeed they are square-integrable.  Equations (1), (3), and (4) prove the lemma.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\) and \(i,j\in\mathbb Z\).  By the exact score-split lemma, \(|Z_i^{(w)}|\le K\), so all products and conditional expectations below are integrable.  Conditional on \(\mathcal F_U\), the graph, exposure maps, and common no-carryover potential-outcome schedule are fixed, and \(Z_i^{(w)}\) is a measurable function of the assignment field \(D^{(w)}\).  Conditional independence of the two assignment waves therefore implies conditional independence of \(Z_i^{(1)}\) and \(Z_j^{(2)}\), even if the corresponding within-wave assignment neighborhoods overlap.  The two waves have the same conditional Bernoulli design.  Thus, by the definition of \(m_i\),
\[
 \mathbb E_P[Z_i^{(1)}Z_j^{(2)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
 =\mathbb E_P[Z_i^{(1)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
  \mathbb E_P[Z_j^{(2)}\mid\mathcal F_U]
 =m_im_j. \tag{1}
\]
The iid-innovation condition together with graph, exposure, and outcome equivariance makes \((m_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}\) stationary.  Consequently \(\mathbb E_Pm_i=\mathbb E_Pm_0=\tau_{\mathrm P}\), and \(h_i=m_i-\tau_{\mathrm P}\) is centered.  Taking expectations in (1), setting \(i=0\) and \(j=k\), and expanding \(m_i=\tau_{\mathrm P}+h_i\) give
\[
 \mathbb E_P[Z_0^{(1)}Z_k^{(2)}]-\tau_{\mathrm P}^2
 =\mathbb E_P[m_0m_k]-\tau_{\mathrm P}^2
 =\mathbb E_P[h_0h_k]
 =\gamma_h(k). \tag{2}
\]
The causal target was defined independently as \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=\sum_{k=-2r}^{2r}\gamma_h(k)\).  Summing (2) over this fixed covariance-support set proves
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}
 =\sum_{k=-2r}^{2r}
 \left\{\mathbb E_P[Z_0^{(1)}Z_k^{(2)}]-\tau_{\mathrm P}^2\right\}.
\]
Thus the observed-law cross-wave moment identifies the already-defined causal functional; the relationship has been derived rather than imposed as a definition.

By radius-\(r\) score locality, conditional expectation integrates a measurable function of \(D_{i-r}^{(w)},\ldots,D_{i+r}^{(w)}\) against its finite product Bernoulli law.  Hence \(m_i\), and therefore \(h_i\), is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(U_{i-r},\ldots,U_{i+r})\).  The equivariance assumptions and iid innovation law make \((h_i)_{i\in\mathbb Z}\) stationary, while the definition of \(\tau_{\mathrm P}\) makes it centered.  The score envelope implies square integrability.  Thus \(h_i\) is a centered \((2r+1)\)-block factor, and \(h_i\) and \(h_j\) are independent whenever \(|i-j|>2r\).

For \(M>2r\), stationarity and finite dependence give the exact covariance expansion
\[
 \frac1M\operatorname{Var}_P\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^M h_i\right)
 =\gamma_h(0)+2\sum_{k=1}^{2r}
 \left(1-\frac{k}{M}\right)\gamma_h(k). \tag{1}
\]
Letting \(M\to\infty\) in this finite sum yields
\[
 \lim_{M\to\infty}\frac1M
 \operatorname{Var}_P\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^M h_i\right)
 =\gamma_h(0)+2\sum_{k=1}^{2r}\gamma_h(k)
 =\sum_{k=-2r}^{2r}\gamma_h(k)
 =\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}. \tag{2}
\]
Every variance on the left of (2) is nonnegative, so \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge0\).

Apply the cited finite-block coboundary theorem \(\text{lem:janson-block-factor-coboundary}\) with block length \(2r+1\), after reindexing the input block \((U_{i-r},\ldots,U_{i+r})\).  Its hypotheses hold by the preceding paragraph and (2).  Because \(h_i\) is centered, the cited theorem says that \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\) if and only if there is a square-integrable \(2r\)-block factor
\[
 g_i=g(U_{i-r+1},\ldots,U_{i+r})
 \quad\text{such that}\quad
 h_i=g_i-g_{i-1}\quad P\text{-almost surely}. \tag{3}
\]
Under (3), telescoping gives, without an approximation,
\[
 \sum_{i\in I_n}h_i
 =\sum_{i=r+1}^{n-r}(g_i-g_{i-1})
 =g_{n-r}-g_r,
 \qquad
 \frac1{N_n}\sum_{i\in I_n}h_i
 =\frac{g_{n-r}-g_r}{N_n}. \tag{4}
\]
For \(n>4r\), \(g_r\) is a function of \((U_1,\ldots,U_{2r})\), whereas \(g_{n-r}\) is a function of \((U_{n-2r+1},\ldots,U_n)\).  These innovation blocks are disjoint.  The iid condition makes the endpoints independent, and stationarity gives each the law of \(g_0\).  Therefore, for every \(n>4r\), the right side of the first identity in (4) already has the law of \(g^\star-g_0\).  In particular,
\[
 \sum_{i\in I_n}h_i\Rightarrow g^\star-g_0.
\]

Fix \(n>4r\), \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).  Apply the already-established fixed-footprint Cayley/F\o lner concentration theorem \(\text{thm:folner-fixed-footprint-two-wave-concentration}\) to the additive group \(\Gamma=\mathbb Z\), with
\[
 A=\{-r,\ldots,r\},
 \qquad C=A-A=\{-2r,\ldots,2r\}.
\]
Then \(a=|A|=2r+1\), \(q=|C|=4r+1\), \(\Lambda=\Lambda_n\), and the theorem's interior \(I\) is \(I_n\).  Its pair sets are \(J_{n,k}\), and
\[
 N=N_n=n-2r,
 \qquad
 \nu=\min_{|k|\le2r}N_{n,k}=n-4r>0,
 \qquad |\Lambda|=n. \tag{1}
\]

We verify the theorem's primitive premises.  Score locality says that the score at \(i\) depends only on \((U_j,D_j^{(w)})_{i-r\le j\le i+r}\), so the footprint is exactly the fixed set \(A\).  Exposure and outcome equivariance give the common translation-equivariant score rule.  The exact score-split lemma and exposure positivity give \(|Z_i^{(w)}|\le K=B/\varepsilon<\infty\).  The wavewise Bernoulli condition supplies the product assignment law in each wave, and cross-wave independence supplies its conditional factorization across waves.  Since the conditional product law has the fixed parameter \(p\) and does not depend on the value of \(U\), for cylinder events \(A_U,B_1,B_2\),
\[
 P\{U\in A_U,D^{(1)}\in B_1,D^{(2)}\in B_2\}
 =P(U\in A_U)\,\mu_p(B_1)\,\mu_p(B_2), \tag{2}
\]
where \(\mu_p\) is the product \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) law.  Thus the iid innovation coordinates and the two assignment-coordinate families have the independence required by the fixed-footprint theorem.  The buffered-coupling proposition identifies its finite local scores with \(Z_{n,i}^{(w)}\) on \(I_n\), and the cross-wave-identification lemma identifies its population functional \(\Omega\) with the causal target \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\).

Specializing the theorem's bias allowance using (1) gives
\[
 \frac{4q^2K^2}{N}
 =\frac{4(4r+1)^2K^2}{N_n}=b_n, \tag{3}
\]
and its deviation allowance becomes
\[
 \frac{\sqrt{48|\Lambda|}\,a qK^2}{\nu}
 \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 =\frac{\sqrt{48n}(2r+1)(4r+1)K^2}{n-4r}
 \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 =q_n(\delta). \tag{4}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 P\!\left\{|\widehat\Omega_n^{12}-\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}|
       >b_n+q_n(\delta)\right\}\le\delta. \tag{5}
\]
The right side and both allowances depend on \(P\) only through the common class constants \(r,B,\varepsilon\).  Taking the supremum of (5) over \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\) proves the stated uniform inequality.

For the prescribed finite-instance stress test, take \(r=1\), \(n=5\), the deterministic line graph, \(E_i(d,G)=d_i\), \(p=1/2\), and \(Y_i(d;U,G)=Bd_i\).  Then \(N_n=3\), \(Z_i^{(w)}=2BD_i^{(w)}\), \(m_i=B\), \(h_i=0\), and \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\).  Over each of the \(2^{10}\) two-wave assignment vectors, every lag-product average and product of wave means belongs to \([0,4B^2]\), so \(|\widehat\Omega_n^{12}|\le20B^2\).  Because \(\varepsilon<1/2\), \(K=B/\varepsilon>2B\), and hence
\[
 b_n=\frac{4\cdot25K^2}{3}>\frac{400B^2}{3}>20B^2.
\]
Thus no assignment rejects at this smallest admissible \(r=1\) volume, and direct averaging over all assignments gives \(\mathbb E_P\widehat\Omega_n^{12}=0\), consistently with the bias identity used above.

Write \(F_n=\widehat\Omega_n^{12}\).  Under any \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\) with \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\), rejection entails
\[
 |F_n-\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}|=|F_n|
 >b_n+q_n(\alpha)=t_n(\alpha).
\]
The uniform concentration theorem with \(\delta=\alpha\) therefore gives \(P(\phi_{n,\alpha}=1)\le\alpha\), uniformly over the null class.

Now suppose
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)
 =2b_n+q_n(\alpha)+q_n(\beta).
\]
On nonrejection, \(F_n\le b_n+q_n(\alpha)\), and consequently
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}-F_n
 \ge \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}-b_n-q_n(\alpha)
 \ge b_n+q_n(\beta). \tag{1}
\]
For every \(\beta'\in(\beta,1)\), the function \(q_n(\cdot)\) is strictly decreasing.  Hence (1) implies
\[
 |F_n-\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}|>b_n+q_n(\beta').
\]
The concentration theorem with \(\delta=\beta'\) gives \(P(\phi_{n,\alpha}=0)\le\beta'\).  Letting \(\beta'\downarrow\beta\) proves \(P(\phi_{n,\alpha}=0)\le\beta\), including the non-strict boundary \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)\).

For fixed \(r,B,\varepsilon,\alpha,\beta\), the envelope \(K=B/\varepsilon\) is fixed and \(N_n=n-2r\).  Therefore
\[
 b_n=O(n^{-1}),
 \qquad
 q_n(\delta)
 =\frac{\sqrt{48n}(2r+1)(4r+1)K^2}{n-4r}
 \sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 =O(n^{-1/2})
\]
for fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\).  It follows that \(\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)=O(n^{-1/2})\).

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\), write \(L=4r+1\), \(a_r=2r+1\), \(\ell=2r+1\), and put \(M=N_{n,\ell}=n-4r-1>0\).  By the Janson-boundary proposition, \(h_i\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(U_{i-r},\ldots,U_{i+r})\).  Hence \(h_i\) and \(h_j\) are independent whenever \(|i-j|>2r\).  They are centered by the definitions of \(h_i\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm P}\), so
\[
 \mathbb E_P[h_i h_{i+\ell}]=0. \tag{1}
\]
Cross-wave identification, stationarity, and buffered coupling give, for every \(|k|\le2r\),
\[
 \mathbb E_P\!\left[
 \frac1{N_{n,k}}\sum_{i\in J_{n,k}}
 Z_{n,i}^{(1)}Z_{n,i+k}^{(2)}
 \right]
 =\mathbb E_P[m_0m_k]
 =\tau_{\mathrm P}^2+\gamma_h(k). \tag{2}
\]
The same argument at lag \(\ell\), followed by (1), gives
\[
 \mathbb E_P\!\left[
 \frac1{N_{n,\ell}}\sum_{i\in J_{n,\ell}}
 Z_{n,i}^{(1)}Z_{n,i+\ell}^{(2)}
 \right]=\tau_{\mathrm P}^2. \tag{3}
\]
Subtracting \(L\) copies of (3) from the sum of (2) over \(-2r\le k\le2r\) proves the exact identity
\[
 \mathbb E_P[\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}]
 =\sum_{k=-2r}^{2r}\gamma_h(k)
 =\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}. \tag{4}
\]

We next derive the deviation bound from independent primitive coordinates.  The fixed conditional \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) product law and cross-wave conditional independence imply, for cylinder events \(A,B,C\),
\[
 P\{U\in A,D^{(1)}\in B,D^{(2)}\in C\}
 =P\{U\in A\}\,P\{D^{(1)}\in B\}\,P\{D^{(2)}\in C\}.
\]
Together with iid innovations, this shows that the \(3n\) coordinates
\(U_1,\ldots,U_n,D_1^{(1)},\ldots,D_n^{(1)},D_1^{(2)},\ldots,D_n^{(2)}\)
are mutually independent.  Score locality implies that changing one environmental coordinate changes at most \(a_r\) retained scores in each wave, whereas changing one assignment coordinate changes at most \(a_r\) retained scores in its own wave.  The exact score-split envelope and buffered coupling give \(|Z_{n,i}^{(w)}|\le K\); changing either factor can therefore change a product by at most \(2K^2\).

At a fixed lag \(|k|\le2r\), changing one environmental coordinate affects at most \(2a_r\) products.  Since \(N_{n,k}\ge n-4r>M\), the sum of the \(L\) short-lag averages changes by at most \(4a_rLK^2/(n-4r)\).  The lag-\(\ell\) average, after multiplication by \(L\), changes by at most \(4a_rLK^2/M\).  Hence the total environmental-coordinate oscillation is at most
\[
 4a_rLK^2\left\{\frac1{n-4r}+\frac1M\right\}
 \le \frac{8a_rLK^2}{M}. \tag{5}
\]
For an assignment coordinate only one factor in each affected product changes.  The same count gives total oscillation at most
\[
 2a_rLK^2\left\{\frac1{n-4r}+\frac1M\right\}
 \le \frac{4a_rLK^2}{M}. \tag{6}
\]
Set \(c=a_rLK^2/M\).  Summing squared oscillations over the \(n\) environmental and \(2n\) assignment coordinates yields
\[
 n(8c)^2+2n(4c)^2=96nc^2. \tag{7}
\]
The cited McDiarmid bounded-differences lemma, applied with arbitrarily enlarged strict oscillation bounds and then by taking the enlargement down to zero, gives
\[
 P\!\left\{\left|\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}
 -\mathbb E_P\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}\right|>t\right\}
 \le2\exp\!\left\{-\frac{t^2}{48nc^2}\right\}. \tag{8}
\]
Taking
\[
 t=\sqrt{48n}\,c\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)}
 =q_n^{\mathrm u}(\delta)
\]
in (8) and using (4) proves the asserted concentration inequality.

If \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0\), rejection implies a deviation strictly larger than \(q_n^{\mathrm u}(\alpha)\), so (8) gives size at most \(\alpha\).  If \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge q_n^{\mathrm u}(\alpha)+q_n^{\mathrm u}(\beta)\), nonrejection implies \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}-\widehat\Omega_n^{\mathrm u}\ge q_n^{\mathrm u}(\beta)\).  For every \(\beta'>\beta\), strict monotonicity of \(q_n^{\mathrm u}(\cdot)\) turns this into a deviation strictly exceeding \(q_n^{\mathrm u}(\beta')\); (8) bounds its probability by \(\beta'\).  Letting \(\beta'\downarrow\beta\) proves power at least \(1-\beta\).  Finally, for fixed \(r,B,\varepsilon,\alpha,\beta\), the displayed formula for \(q_n^{\mathrm u}\) is \(O(n^{-1/2})\), and (4) shows that no sample-centering bias allowance is present.

We first prove the upper bound.  By the definition of the canonical full observation, there is a fixed Borel map \(T_n\) such that \(W_n=T_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\): every score is computed from one realized outcome, its exposure indicators, and the two strictly positive known propensity coordinates.  Hence \(\widehat\Omega_n^{12}\), and therefore \(\phi_{n,\alpha}\), is a common Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\).  The two-wave size-and-separation theorem gives, uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\),
\[
 \mathbb E_P[\phi_{n,\alpha}]\le\alpha
 \quad\text{if }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_P[1-\phi_{n,\alpha}]\le\beta
 \quad\text{if }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge\rho_n(\alpha,\beta).
\]
The definition of \(s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) therefore implies
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}
 \le\rho_n(\alpha,\beta). \tag{1}
\]

For the converse, we construct an exact-local, causal-realizable, common-support submodel.  Fix \(a\in(0,2B]\) and set \(b=a/2\), so \(0<b\le B\).  Let the graph be the deterministic nearest-neighbor line, let the innovations be iid \(\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\), and define
\[
 E_i(d,G)=
 \begin{cases}
 e_1,&d_i=1,\\
 e_0,&d_i=0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 C_i(d)=(d_i,d_{i+1})\in\mathcal C:=\{00,01,10,11\}.
\]
Draw the two assignment waves conditionally independently, with iid \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) coordinates.  The innovation \(U_i\) generates a random four-cell schedule
\(V_i=(V_{i,00},V_{i,01},V_{i,10},V_{i,11})\in\{-b,b\}^4\), independently across sites.  Define
\[
 \mathcal H_0
 =\{v\in\{-b,b\}^4:v_{10}+v_{11}-v_{00}-v_{01}=0\}.
\]
There are six schedules in \(\mathcal H_0\).  Let \(Q_0\) be uniform on \(\mathcal H_0\), put
\[
 v^+=(-b,-b,b,b),
 \qquad v^-=-v^+,
\]
in coordinate order \((00,01,10,11)\), let \(Q_1\) put mass \(1/2\) on each of \(v^+,v^-\), and, for \(0\le t<1\), set
\[
 Q_t=(1-t)Q_0+tQ_1. \tag{2}
\]
A finite quantile partition of \([0,1]\) realizes each \(Q_t\) as a measurable function of \(U_i\).  Under the resulting law \(P_t\), define the common no-carryover potential-outcome schedule by
\[
 Y_i(d;U,G)=V_{i,C_i(d)}. \tag{3}
\]
The line graph is shift equivariant and has edge range one.  Because \(r\) is a positive integer, the exposure and outcome rules in (3), which depend only on \((U_i,d_i,d_{i+1})\), are radius-\(r\) local.  They are shift equivariant.  Also \(|Y_i|=b\le B\), and
\(\pi_i(e_1)=\pi_i(e_0)=1/2\ge\varepsilon\) because \(\varepsilon<1/2\).  The iid innovations and the two independent Bernoulli waves verify the remaining class conditions.  Thus \(P_t\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\) for every \(0\le t<1\).

Given \(V_i=v\), direct averaging over the four equiprobable local assignment cells gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 m_i
 &=\mathbb E_{P_t}\!\left[
 Y_i(D^{(w)};U,G)
 \left\{\frac{\mathbf 1(D_i^{(w)}=1)}{1/2}
 -\frac{\mathbf 1(D_i^{(w)}=0)}{1/2}\right\}
 \middle|\mathcal F_U\right]\\
 &=\frac{v_{10}+v_{11}-v_{00}-v_{01}}2.
 \end{aligned} \tag{4}
\]
Thus \(m_i=0\) on \(\mathcal H_0\), while (4) equals \(a\) at \(v^+\) and \(-a\) at \(v^-\).  Symmetry of \(Q_t\) gives \(\tau_{\mathrm P}=\mathbb E_{P_t}m_i=0\).  The schedules are iid across sites, so \((h_i)=(m_i)\) is iid, and
\[
 \gamma_h(0)=\mathbb E_{P_t}m_i^2=a^2t,
 \qquad
 \gamma_h(k)=0\quad(k\ne0),
 \qquad
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}(P_t)=a^2t. \tag{5}
\]
In particular, \(P_0\) is a null law and \(P_t\) is an alternative for \(t>0\).  Equation (4) verifies that (5) changes the causal conditional exposure-effect score, not merely an arbitrary observed-law functional.

We now bound the information in the complete declared observation.  Condition on both assignment arrays.  At site \(i\), the two observed outcomes select the ordered cell pair \((c,c')=(C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)}))\).  Let \(R_j^{c,c'}\) denote the law of \((V_{i,c},V_{i,c'})\) under \(Q_j\), for \(j\in\{0,1\}\), and list probabilities in atom order \((b,b),(b,-b),(-b,b),(-b,-b)\).  Exhaustive enumeration of the six schedules in \(\mathcal H_0\) and the two schedules \(v^+,v^-\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{ordered cell pair}&R_0^{c,c'}&R_1^{c,c'}\\ \hline
c=c'&(1/2,0,0,1/2)&(1/2,0,0,1/2)\\
c\ne c'\text{ within }\{00,01\}\text{ or }\{10,11\}
 &(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)&(1/2,0,0,1/2)\\
c\text{ and }c'\text{ in opposite exposure groups}
 &(1/3,1/6,1/6,1/3)&(0,1/2,1/2,0).
\end{array} \tag{6}
\]
These three rows cover all sixteen ordered pairs in \(\mathcal C^2\), so (6) is also the exact finite-cell stress test.  Every atom charged by \(R_1^{c,c'}\) has positive \(R_0^{c,c'}\)-probability.  Therefore the two-wave observed-outcome law has common support, even though the latent four-cell schedule law in (2) does not.

Put \(R_t^{c,c'}=(1-t)R_0^{c,c'}+tR_1^{c,c'}\).  For distinct cells, direct substitution in (6) gives
\[
 \sum_x\frac{\{R_1^{c,c'}(x)-R_0^{c,c'}(x)\}^2}
 {R_0^{c,c'}(x)}=2, \tag{7}
\]
whereas the quantity is zero for \(c=c'\).  Since \(\log u\le u-1\) for \(u>0\), absolute continuity and (7) imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \operatorname{KL}(R_t^{c,c'}\Vert R_0^{c,c'})
 &\le \sum_x
 \frac{\{R_t^{c,c'}(x)-R_0^{c,c'}(x)\}^2}
 {R_0^{c,c'}(x)}\\
 &\le2t^2.
 \end{aligned} \tag{8}
\]
Conditional on the assignments, the selected outcome pairs are independent over \(i\in I_n\), because the schedules \(V_i\) are independent.  The graph and assignment laws are identical under \(P_t\) and \(P_0\); exposures and propensity coordinates are deterministic functions of them.  The likelihood chain rule for these finite product measures, followed by (8), therefore gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\operatorname{KL}\!\left(
 \mathcal L_{P_t}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})
 \middle\Vert
 \mathcal L_{P_0}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\right)\\
 &\quad=\mathbb E_D\sum_{i\in I_n}
 \operatorname{KL}\!\left(
 R_t^{C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)})}
 \middle\Vert
 R_0^{C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)})}\right)
 \le2N_nt^2. 
 \end{aligned} \tag{9}
\]
Thus (9) controls the entire observed record, not only its score coordinates.

Let \(\eta=1-\alpha-\beta>0\) and set
\[
 t_0=\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{2N_n}}.
\]
Because \(0<\eta<1\) and \(N_n\ge1\), one has \(0<t_0<1\), so \(P_{t_0}\) belongs to the submodel.  The cited Pinsker inequality and (9) imply
\[
 \operatorname{TV}\!\left(
 \mathcal L_{P_{t_0}}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}),
 \mathcal L_{P_0}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\right)
 \le\sqrt{N_nt_0^2}
 =\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}. \tag{10}
\]
Let \(\varphi_n\in\Phi_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\) be any randomized test satisfying \(\mathbb E_{P_0}\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\le\alpha\).  To apply the binary form of the cited Le Cam testing lemma, adjoin under both laws a common independent \(A\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) and reject if \(A\le\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Taking a product with the same uniform law preserves total variation.  The Le Cam lemma and (10) then yield
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_{t_0}}[1-\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})]
 \ge1-\alpha-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}
 =\beta+\eta\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)
 >\beta. \tag{11}
\]
By (5),
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}(P_{t_0})
 =\frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}. \tag{12}
\]
For every candidate separation not exceeding (12), \(P_{t_0}\) belongs to the alternative set and violates the required type-II bound in (11).  Hence every feasible separation is strictly larger than (12), and taking the infimum in the definition of \(s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) proves the displayed lower bound.  Combining it with (1), choosing any fixed \(a\in(0,2B]\), using \(N_n=n-2r\), and invoking the proved rate \(\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)=O(n^{-1/2})\) establishes \(s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\Theta(n^{-1/2})\).  If \(e_1=e_0\), every score cancels identically, which explains why distinct focal labels are required.

Set \(r=1\) and use the two laws specified in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}boundary\text{-}witnesses}\).  The innovation state space may be taken to be the Borel set \(\{-1,1\}\), and under either law the coordinates \(U_i\) are independent Rademacher variables.  In particular,
\[
 \mathbb E_P[U_i]=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_P[U_i^2]=1,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_P[U_iU_j]=0\quad(i\ne j).
\]
Thus the innovation condition in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}two\text{-}wave\text{-}local\text{-}class}\) holds.

We first verify the remaining membership conditions in that definition.  The deterministic nearest-neighbor line is invariant under every integer shift, and every neighbor of \(i\) is in \(\{i-1,i+1\}\subseteq\{i-1,i,i+1\}\), so graph equivariance and graph range one hold.  For the common exposure rule,
\[
 E_{i+k}(d,G)=d_{i+k}=(\theta^k d)_i=E_i(\theta^k d,\theta^kG),
\]
so exposure equivariance holds.  Write
\[
 X_i^{\Delta}=U_i-U_{i-1},
 \qquad
 X_i^{+}=U_i.
\]
The two schedules are \(Y_i(d;U,G)=X_i^{\Delta}d_i\) and \(Y_i(d;U,G)=X_i^{+}d_i\), respectively.  For either choice \(\circ\in\{\Delta,+\}\), direct substitution and the definition of \(\theta\) give
\[
 Y_{i+k}(d;U,G)
 =X_{i+k}^{\circ}d_{i+k}
 =Y_i(\theta^kd;\theta^kU,\theta^kG),
\]
which verifies outcome equivariance.  Moreover, \(E_i(d,G)\) and either outcome are measurable with respect to
\[
 \sigma(U_j,d_j:i-1\le j\le i+1),
\]
because they use only \(d_i\) and, respectively, \((U_{i-1},U_i)\) or \(U_i\).  Hence the score-locality condition holds.  Since \(d_i\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
 |X_i^{\Delta}d_i|
 \le |U_i|+|U_{i-1}|=2,
 \qquad
 |X_i^{+}d_i|\le |U_i|=1.
\]
The assumed inequality \(B\ge2\) therefore gives the common outcome envelope under both laws.

By the assignment part of Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}boundary\text{-}witnesses}\), conditional on \(\mathcal F_U\), each wave consists of independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p)\) coordinates and the two waves are conditionally independent.  Since \(E_i(d,G)=d_i\), \(e_1=1\), and \(e_0=0\), the conditional exposure probabilities are
\[
 \pi_i(e_1)
 =P(D_i^{(w)}=1\mid\mathcal F_U)=p,
 \qquad
 \pi_i(e_0)
 =P(D_i^{(w)}=0\mid\mathcal F_U)=1-p.
\]
The assumed inequality \(\varepsilon\le\min\{p,1-p\}\), together with \(0<p<1\), verifies exposure positivity and makes both divisions in the score well defined.  We have now checked every membership condition in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}two\text{-}wave\text{-}local\text{-}class}\), and consequently
\[
 P^{\Delta},P^+\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}
 \quad\text{when }r=1.
\]

It remains to compute the two population variances.  Under either witness, let \(X_i\) denote the corresponding \(X_i^{\Delta}\) or \(X_i^+\).  For each wave \(w\), the exposure-IPW score definition and the identities \((D_i^{(w)})^2=D_i^{(w)}\) and \(D_i^{(w)}(1-D_i^{(w)})=0\) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 Z_i^{(w)}
 &=X_iD_i^{(w)}
 \left\{
   \frac{D_i^{(w)}}p
   -\frac{1-D_i^{(w)}}{1-p}
 \right\} \\
 &=X_i\frac{D_i^{(w)}}p.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(X_i\) is \(\mathcal F_U\)-measurable, while the Bernoulli design gives \(\mathbb E_P[D_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U]=p\).  Therefore the definition of \(m_i\) implies
\[
 m_i=\mathbb E_P[Z_i^{(w)}\mid\mathcal F_U]=X_i.
\]
The displayed Rademacher moments give \(\mathbb E_P[X_i]=0\) under both witnesses.  Hence, by the definitions of \(\tau_{\mathrm P}\) and \(h_i\),
\[
 \tau_{\mathrm P}=\mathbb E_P[m_0]=0,
 \qquad
 h_i=m_i-\tau_{\mathrm P}=X_i.
\]

For \(P^{\Delta}\), this proves \(h_i=U_i-U_{i-1}\).  Expanding each product and using independence and the three Rademacher moment identities above gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \gamma_h(0)
 &=\mathbb E_P[(U_0-U_{-1})^2]=1+1=2,\\
 \gamma_h(1)
 &=\mathbb E_P[(U_0-U_{-1})(U_1-U_0)]=-1,\\
 \gamma_h(-1)
 &=\mathbb E_P[(U_0-U_{-1})(U_{-1}-U_{-2})]=-1,\\
 \gamma_h(2)&=\gamma_h(-2)=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because \(r=1\), the definition of \(\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\) consequently yields
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}
 =\sum_{k=-2}^{2}\gamma_h(k)
 =0-1+2-1+0=0.
\]
Notice that this is a covariance cancellation rather than homogeneity: \(\mathbb E_P[h_i^2]=2>0\).

For \(P^+\), the same calculation already showed \(h_i=U_i\).  Independence and centering give
\[
 \gamma_h(0)=\mathbb E_P[U_0^2]=1,
 \qquad
 \gamma_h(k)=\mathbb E_P[U_0U_k]=0\quad(k\ne0).
\]
Summing the five lags prescribed when \(r=1\) gives
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=1.
\]
This proves all asserted membership, score, and population-variance claims for the two witnesses.
